High priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur and daughter of Sargon of Akkad, active around 2285 to 2250 BCE. She is often called the earliest author in history known by name; the chart shows the years she was active.

Sargon put her in this old Sumerian post to bind the cities of the south to his new Akkadian Empire. Hymns credited to her, written in Sumerian cuneiform, praise the goddess Inanna in a personal voice. One poem tells how a rebel drove her out of Ur and how she was later restored, probably under her nephew Naram-Sin. A cycle of 42 temple hymns to the shrines of the Sumerian cities is also given to her.

Her works survive in copies made centuries later by Babylonian scribes, who studied them in school, so some scholars doubt she wrote them herself. A carved alabaster disc found at Ur in the 1920s shows her leading an offering.
